clue.text: Clamour after a boy hit piano — it's only a pantomime prop!

parts.note: taken as written
a lad is a boy
a din is a loud clamour; 'after' puts it behind the boy
to slam is to hit hard
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: Somebody bangs a piano noisily, and the scene is dismissed as mere pantomime business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' is a positional word: the clamour follows 'a boy'. Pantomime is the British Christmas stage show, where Aladdin is a staple story.
explanation.definitionFit: The magic lamp Aladdin rubs to summon the genie is a stock stage property in the Christmas pantomime of that tale.

clue.text: Mean army's first to penetrate a border

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to penetrate is to go inside, so this letter goes within the border

parts.note: a verge is a border or edge

indicators.note: first picks out only the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: the opening letter of army

explanation.surface: A nasty army leads an invasion across a frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' suggests cruelty, but it is the arithmetic mean. A goes inside VERGE after the opening A.
explanation.definitionFit: The mean of a set of numbers is its average, the sum divided by the count.

clue.text: A star not good in Shakespearean role

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: not good says the letter for good is taken out of the star's name

parts.note: Rigel is a bright star in Orion
g is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A celebrity actor gives a poor showing in a Shakespeare part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'star' suggests a famous actor, but it is the astronomical Rigel, which loses G.
explanation.definitionFit: Ariel is the airy spirit who serves Prospero in Shakespeare's The Tempest, a well-known role.

clue.text: Setter is taken in by wicked figure of French harlots?

indicators.note: being taken in by something means being held inside it, so the setter's phrase sits within the wicked figure

parts.note: a demon is an evil being
the setter says I'm, so I'M stands for 'setter is'
de is French for of

explanation.surface: The setter admits being fooled by a sinful character among French courtesans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter is' stands for I'M, the setter speaking of themself; it splits the wicked figure after its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The demi-monde was the class of kept women of dubious reputation in nineteenth-century France, hence the question mark for harlots.

clue.text: Dark times in France requiring removal of current idiots

indicators.note: requiring removal means one letter must be taken out of the French word

parts.note: nuits is French for nights
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: Power cuts in France bring dark nights, blamed on idiots.
explanation.walkthrough: NUITS without I leaves NUTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuts is informal for crazy people, and in plural noun use it can stand for idiots or cranks.

clue.text: Not how to describe this entry in essentially athletic sport

indicators.note: in places one element inside the other, so the description sits within the central letters
essentially points to the essence, the very centre, so only the middle letters are kept

parts.note: the two central letters of athletic

parts.words: Not how to describe this entry
parts.note: this entry is a down light, so 'across' is the wrong label for it

explanation.surface: A puzzling remark that some sport isn't the right description for this athletic pursuit.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue refers to its own grid position: it runs down, so the direction it is not is the other one.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacrosse is a team sport played with netted sticks, originally from North America.

clue.text: Ruminant — like a crab? That's not right

indicators.note: not right says the abbreviation for right is missing from the word

parts.note: a crab is a grumpy person, so morose describes one
r is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone guesses that a cud-chewing animal resembles a crab, then admits the comparison is wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crab' looks like the crustacean but means a sour, grumpy person.
explanation.definitionFit: A moose is a large deer, and deer chew the cud, so it is a ruminant.

clue.text: Violinist sending up one note in a lull

indicators.note: in a down entry, sending up means writing from the bottom upwards, so the whole run is reversed

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
n is the abbreviation for note
taken as written
taken as written
a gap is a lull or pause

explanation.surface: A violinist mocks a single quiet note played during a lull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sending up' suggests mockery but means reverse: I N IN A GAP turned over gives PAGANINI.
explanation.definitionFit: Niccolo Paganini was the celebrated Italian virtuoso of the violin in the early nineteenth century.

clue.text: Believe online forum half-heartedly supporting Conservative

indicators.note: with half its heart gone, one of the two doubled middle letters is lost

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative; 'supporting' places it beneath in a down entry
Reddit is a well-known online discussion forum

explanation.surface: Someone half-trusts an internet forum because it backs the Tories.
explanation.walkthrough: REDDIT loses one of its central Ds, and in a down entry 'supporting' means sitting under C.
explanation.definitionFit: To credit a story is to believe it, a straight synonym as a verb.

clue.text: Mysterious quote provided over morning drink recalled

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the whole assembled string is read backwards
something provided over another thing is laid round it, so the quote wraps the drink

parts.note: to cite is to quote
a.m. stands for the morning
gin is a drink

explanation.surface: Someone offers a cryptic quotation about an early-morning tipple, half remembered.
explanation.walkthrough: CITE wraps AMGIN to make CITAMGINE, which read backwards is ENIGMATIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Enigmatic describes something puzzling and hard to interpret, a direct synonym of mysterious.

clue.text: Broadcasting feasible? Duo missing page

parts.note: 'on' means feasible or doable, as in 'that's not on'

indicators.note: missing says a letter is absent, so the word for a duo loses the page abbreviation

parts.note: a duo is a pair
p is the abbreviation for page

explanation.surface: A producer asks whether a broadcast is possible now a duo of presenters has lost its page.
explanation.walkthrough: 'feasible' here is the sense of 'on' in 'that's just not on'.
explanation.definitionFit: A programme that is on air is being transmitted, which is what broadcasting means as an adjective.

clue.text: Old man returned high shot, possessing male assurance

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the word for old man is read backwards

parts.note: pa is a father, one's old man

indicators.note: possessing means holding inside, so the high shot holds the letter for male

parts.note: a lob is a high shot, as in tennis
M is the abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: A father hits back a lofty shot with masculine confidence, as in a game of tennis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old man' is a familiar term for one's father.
explanation.definitionFit: Aplomb is self-confident poise, close to assurance in the sense of composure.

clue.text: Poet's written about single year in place like that inspiring Gray's "Elegy"

indicators.note: being written about places one word around another, so the poet surrounds the single year

parts.note: a bard is a poet; the 's is 'is'
one is single
y is the abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: A literary note on a poet who wrote about one year spent at the churchyard that inspired a famous elegy.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Gray's 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard' is the poem meant, so the definition points to a graveyard.
explanation.definitionFit: Boneyard is an informal word for a cemetery or graveyard, the kind of country churchyard that prompted Gray's poem.

clue.text: Decide to dispatch detective to get something linked to peer?

indicators.note: to dispatch is to send away, so the detective's abbreviation is removed from the word for decide

parts.note: to determine is to decide
Det is the abbreviation for detective

explanation.surface: An order to send a detective away so as to obtain some connection to a lord.
explanation.walkthrough: DETERMINE minus DET leaves ERMINE. A peer is a member of the British nobility.
explanation.definitionFit: Ermine fur trims the ceremonial robes worn by peers in the House of Lords, so it is associated with them.

clue.text: French composer's religious work covering doctrine with no overture

indicators.note: an overture opens a work, so with no overture the opening letter is lost

parts.note: a mass is a religious service or a musical setting of one; 'covering' places it above in a down entry
a tenet is a doctrine

explanation.surface: A French composer's sacred piece deals with doctrine but lacks an opening overture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overture' fits the musical scene but just means first letter. TENET loses T, under MASS.
explanation.definitionFit: Jules Massenet was a French composer of operas such as Manon and Werther.

clue.text: Unrealistic remit leader dropped, adopting better

indicators.note: to adopt is to take in, so the shortened word takes the word for better inside it
a leader dropped means the opening letter is lost from the word for remit

parts.note: to remit is to cease or desist
to cap is to better or outdo

explanation.surface: Someone with an unrealistic brief drops the boss and takes on a superior instead.
explanation.walkthrough: Remit here is the verb meaning to slacken or stop, and better is a verb too, as in 'to cap that story'.
explanation.definitionFit: An escapist seeks refuge from reality, and the word is used as an adjective for unrealistic, fantasy-driven fare.

clue.text: Warning signal — rigs struggling — material washed up ashore?

parts.note: amber is the warning light on traffic signals

indicators.note: something struggling is thrown about and disordered, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An alert as oil rigs struggle in a storm, with debris washing onto the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: AMBER followed by RIGS rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambergris is a waxy substance from sperm whales, often found floating at sea or washed up on beaches.

clue.text: Cut sound before satire involving King's language

indicators.note: sound means the word for cut is taken as it is spoken, not spelled

parts.note: sawn means cut, and in a non-rhotic accent it sounds like 'san'

indicators.note: involving means wrapping round, so the satire takes the King's letter within it

parts.note: a skit is a short satirical sketch
R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A cut recording runs before a satire about the monarch's way of speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King's language' seems to be one phrase, but the definition is only 'language'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sanskrit is the ancient classical language of India, used in Hindu scripture.

clue.text: Methodist converted Lewes once, no coming back after that

indicators.note: converted means changed into another form, so the town's letters are rearranged

parts.note: the Sussex town, taken as letters

indicators.note: coming back means heading the other way, so the old word for no is read backwards

parts.note: nay is an archaic word for no

explanation.surface: A tale of a Methodist who converted the town of Lewes and never returned.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewes is a county town in Sussex; 'converted' suits a missionary, but it only rearranges the letters. 'once' marks the old-fashioned no.
explanation.definitionFit: Wesleyan names the Methodist movement founded by John Wesley, so a Wesleyan is a Methodist.

clue.text: Deer a quarry in Wisconsin

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another, so the quarry goes inside the state abbreviation

parts.note: WI is the postal abbreviation for Wisconsin
a pit is a quarry, a hole dug for stone

explanation.surface: A deer is the hunter's quarry in Wisconsin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quarry' suggests hunted prey, fitting the deer, but here it is a stone pit.
explanation.definitionFit: The wapiti is the North American elk, a large species of deer.

clue.text: Irish writer's former schoolfellow getting nothing in Paris

parts.note: OB is old boy, a former pupil of a school
rien is French for nothing

explanation.surface: An Irish author's old classmate ends up with nothing in the French capital.
explanation.walkthrough: An old boy (OB) is a British term for a former pupil of a school.
explanation.definitionFit: Flann O'Brien and Edna O'Brien are both noted Irish novelists, so the surname fits an Irish writer.

clue.text: Inappropriate behaviour around street — police initially unrelenting

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the inappropriate behaviour wraps the street abbreviation

parts.note: a no-no is something not to be done
St is the abbreviation for street

indicators.note: initially keeps only the first letter of the word before it

parts.note: the first letter of police

explanation.surface: Antisocial behaviour on a street draws relentless attention from the police.
explanation.walkthrough: A no-no is an informal term for something one must not do.
explanation.definitionFit: Non-stop means continuing without pause, which is what unrelenting describes.

clue.text: Part of dessert, maybe chunk, mostly a reddish colour

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the word for chunk loses its final letter

parts.note: a piece is a chunk
rust is a reddish-brown colour

explanation.surface: A description of a slice of pudding, a largely reddish-brown chunk.
explanation.walkthrough: PIECE minus its last letter gives PIEC, then RUST.
explanation.definitionFit: The pastry casing of a pie is its crust, one component of a pie served as a pudding course.

clue.text: Home of Latin love or lover

parts.note: Latin was the language of ancient Rome
love is zero in tennis, written as O

explanation.surface: A question of where Latin love poetry came from, or who the lover was.
explanation.walkthrough: ROME then O.
explanation.definitionFit: Romeo, from Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet, is used as a general word for an ardent male lover.

clue.text: Stony concretion ultimately like rubble?

parts.note: stony, as in stony-broke, means having no money

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the last letter of that word is kept

parts.note: the final letter of concretion

explanation.surface: A geologist's question about a hard mineral lump that ends up as rubble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stony' and 'concretion' look like geology, but stony is British slang for penniless (stony-broke).
explanation.definitionFit: Rubble is fragments of rock or masonry, material in a broken state, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Significant area occupied by new coffee producer?

indicators.note: being occupied by something means having it inside, so the new letter sits within

parts.note: key means significant or important
a is the abbreviation for area
n is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A major region taken over for a new coffee plantation.
explanation.walkthrough: KEY A with N inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Kenya is an East African country famous for its high-grade arabica coffee exports, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Complacent when some urge only intermittently appears

indicators.note: appearing intermittently means showing up every other time, so alternate letters are kept

parts.note: first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: Someone becomes complacent when their drive only appears in fits and starts.
explanation.definitionFit: Smug means excessively self-satisfied, essentially the same as complacent.

clue.text: Quantity of heat? Expression of doubt after reverse of hot temperature

indicators.note: reverse of means taken the other way round, so the two abbreviations swap order

parts.note: h is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap
t is the abbreviation for temperature
erm is a hesitant noise of uncertainty

explanation.surface: A puzzled query about a heat measurement, voiced with a doubtful noise after the hot tap ran cold.
explanation.walkthrough: H T reversed gives TH, and ERM comes after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A therm is a unit of heat equal to 100,000 British thermal units, once used for gas billing.

clue.text: Using concerning medium, make latest piece for surrealist artist

parts.note: re means concerning
M is the abbreviation for medium, as on clothes
Bill Brandt was a photographer associated with surrealism

explanation.surface: An instruction to finish a surrealist's last work using some suitable medium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surrealist artist' reads as one phrase, but 'surrealist' is Bill Brandt, placed as the latest piece after RE and M; the definition is just 'artist'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rembrandt van Rijn was the great Dutch painter of the seventeenth century, an artist of the first rank.

clue.text: Staff needing a long time and a pound to make mailroom purchase?

parts.note: a staff is a pole or post
an age is a long time
to stamp is to pound with the feet

explanation.surface: An office worker needs ages and a pound coin to buy something in the mailroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a pound' looks like money (the British pound) but is the verb: to stamp.
explanation.definitionFit: A postage stamp is the small adhesive label bought to pay for sending a letter, the obvious mailroom purchase.
